formulation.evidence: The Postulate defines Newtonian spacetime with E an oriented Euclidean affine space and a Cartesian inertial chart as the event map (t,X) ↦ (t,r_t(X)), with each time-slice map an orientation-preserving affine isometry translated at constant velocity. It specifies the quotient cell, finite-depth reference layer, surface graph, potential velocity, units including gas pressure in pascals, curvature and pressure conventions, fixed-bed impermeability, and exact first-order equations. The model remains an adopted idealization with no nonlinear existence, approximation-error, or empirical-validity claim.

scope.evidence: The Postulate is restricted to an adopted inviscid, homogeneous, incompressible, irrotational, constant-density linear model with negligible gas inertia and constant gravity/surface tension. It excludes no-slip, finite-amplitude error claims, solvability, and universal empirical validity.

On $\Omega_0\times I$ the adopted equations and boundary conditions are

$$\Delta_h\phi+\partial_z^2\phi=0,\qquad -h<z<0,$$

$$\partial_z\phi(x,-h,t)=0,$$

$$\partial_t\eta(x,t)=\partial_z\phi(x,0,t),\qquad \partial_t\phi(x,0,t)+g\eta(x,t)-\frac{\gamma}{\rho}\Delta_h\eta(x,t)=0.$$

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex
numbers** by the quotient ring
$$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set
$$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$
Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map
$\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the
field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which
$\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of
[[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.

Let $f:U\to V$ and $g:V\to\mathbb C$, where $U,V\subseteq\mathbb C$ are open. If $f$ is complex differentiable at $a\in U$ and $g$ is complex differentiable at $f(a)$, then $g\circ f$ is complex differentiable at $a$ and

$$ (g\circ f)'(a)=g'(f(a))f'(a). $$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals) converges to a real
number. Together with The reals form a totally ordered field, this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: Complexifying one horizontal coordinate or the time variable gives an affine holomorphic exponent. By [L2] and [L4], the periodic lift of $q_m$ satisfies $\partial_{x_j}q_m=i k_jq_m$ for $j=1,2$ and $\partial_tq_m=-i\omega q_m$.
Substituting $\phi_c=F(z)q_m$ into the bulk equation and dividing by the nonzero factor $q_m$ gives $F''(z)-k^2F(z)=0$ on $(-h,0)$.
Since $q_m\ne0$ by step 2.1, the bottom condition gives $F'(-h)=k\beta=0$, so $\beta=0$ because $k>0$; therefore $F(z)=\alpha\cosh(k(z+h))$.
Substitution into the kinematic condition and cancellation of $q_m$ using step 2.1 gives $-i\omega H=\alpha k\sinh(kh)$.
Since $kh>0$, [L6] gives $\sinh(kh)>0$; also $g+\gamma k^2/\rho>0$. If $\omega=0$, step 6.1 forces $\alpha=0$, and step 6.2 then forces $H=0$, contrary to the mode definition. Thus $\omega\ne0$.
Solve step 6.1 for $\alpha=-i\omega H/(k\sinh(kh))$ and substitute into step 6.2. Using $(-i)^2=-1$ and $H\ne0$ yields $\omega^2=k(g+\gamma k^2/\rho)\tanh(kh)=(gk+(\gamma/\rho)k^3)\tanh(kh)$.

Let $\Lambda:=(gk+(\gamma/\rho)k^3)\tanh(kh)>0$, using $kh>0$ and [L6]. By [L8], $\sqrt\Lambda$ exists and is a positive real number. By [L1], $\omega^2=\Lambda$ implies $(\omega-\sqrt\Lambda)(\omega+\sqrt\Lambda)=0$ and hence $\omega=\pm\sqrt\Lambda$, with the positive real square root. For either root and any $H\ne0$, set $\alpha:=-i\omega H/(k\sinh(kh))$, $F(z):=\alpha\cosh(k(z+h))$, and $\eta_c:=Hq_m$. The definitions and [L5]–[L6] give $F''=k^2F$, $F'(-h)=0$, and step 1.1 gives the required horizontal and time derivatives; step 6.1 holds by construction, while step 6.2 follows from $\omega^2=\Lambda$. These are nonzero modes for both frequencies, and every nonzero mode has one of these frequencies by step 8.1.
By [L3], $q_m$ never vanishes because $\exp(w)\exp(-w)=1$. Differentiating the horizontal identities in step 1.1 once more gives $\Delta_hq_m=-(k_1^2+k_2^2)q_m=-k^2q_m$.

To solve this equation under only $F\in C^2([-h,0],\mathbb C)$, put $y=z+h\in[0,h]$, $\widehat F(y):=F(y-h)$, $\alpha:=F(-h)$, $\beta:=F'(-h)/k$, and $G(y):=\alpha\cosh(ky)+\beta\sinh(ky)$. By [L5], [L6] and the real chain rule, $G''=k^2G$, $G(0)=\widehat F(0)$ and $G'(0)=\widehat F'(0)$. Let $D:=\widehat F-G$ and $U:=D'-kD$; then $D\in C^2$, $D(0)=D'(0)=0$, and the differential equation gives $U'=D''-kD'=-kU$. From [L5] and [L6], $e^{ky}=\cosh(ky)+\sinh(ky)$ and $(e^{ky})'=ke^{ky}$; hence [L7] gives $(e^{ky}U)'=0$. The mean value theorem applied to both components makes $e^{ky}U$ constant, and its value at $0$ is zero. By [L3], $e^{ky}\ne0$, so $U=0$. A second use of [L7] gives $(e^{-ky}D)'=e^{-ky}(D'-kD)=e^{-ky}U=0$; the same mean-value argument and $D(0)=0$ give $D=0$. Thus every $C^2$ solution has the general form $F(z)=\alpha\cosh(k(z+h))+\beta\sinh(k(z+h))$, and this representation is smooth.
Substitution into the dynamic condition, using $\Delta_h\eta_c=-k^2\eta_c$ from step 2.1 and canceling $q_m\ne0$, gives $-i\omega\alpha\cosh(kh)+(g+\gamma k^2/\rho)H=0$.

citations.quote:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, with absolute time $t\in I$ measured in seconds, and let $E$ be an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean vector space and no origin is distinguished. The Newtonian spacetime is $I\times E$. Define $\mathrm{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. A Cartesian inertial chart is the event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,\mathbf r_t(X))$ for which, at some fixed $t_{\rm ref}\in I$, $\mathbf r_{t_{\rm ref}}:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry whose linear part lies in $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $\mathbf r_t(X)=\mathbf r_{t_{\rm ref}}(X)+w(t-t_{\rm ref})$ for a constant $w\in\mathbb R^3$ in metres per second. Thus each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry; inertial charts are related by $t^*=t+t_0$ and $\mathbf r^*=Q\mathbf r+vt+a$, with constant $t_0$ in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ in metres per second, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ in metres. In the selected chart, $(x_1,x_2,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates in metres, with $x=(x_1,x_2)$ horizontal and $z$ upward; $e_z$ is the upward unit vector.

Fix depth $h>0$ metres and horizontal periods $L_1,L_2>0$ metres, and define $\mathbb T^2_L:=\mathbb R^2/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z)$. A field on this torus is interpreted through its periodic lift $\widetilde f(\widetilde x)=f([\widetilde x])$. For fields on products of this torus with $I$ and $[-h,0]$, $C^r$ means that the lifted field has continuous ordinary coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$, with continuous one-sided extensions at $z=-h,0$. Define $\nabla_h:=(\partial_{x_1},\partial_{x_2})$ and $\Delta_h:=\partial_{x_1}^2+\partial_{x_2}^2$ on the lifts. The real first-order displacement coefficient is $\eta:\mathbb T^2_L\times I\to\mathbb R$, in metres, and the real velocity-potential coefficient is $\phi:\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb R$, in metres squared per second; assume $\eta$ is at least $C^2$ and $\phi$ at least $C^3$ in this sense. Their coefficients are formal and unrestricted in amplitude. Define the fluid-velocity field $u:=\nabla\phi=(\partial_{x_1}\phi,\partial_{x_2}\phi,\partial_z\phi):\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, in metres per second, with no added uniform velocity component. Take constant density $\rho>0$ kilograms per cubic metre, downward gravitational acceleration $-g e_z$ with $g>0$ metres per second squared, and surface tension $\gamma>0$ newtons per metre. The selected model is the first-order capillary free-surface model of the Postulate titled “Linear capillary free-surface model”: its equations on the flat reference slab $\mathbb T^2_L\times(-h,0)$ are

$$\Delta_h\phi+\partial_z^2\phi=0\quad(-h<z<0),\qquad \partial_z\phi(x,-h,t)=0,$$

$$\partial_t\eta(x,t)=\partial_z\phi(x,0,t),\qquad \partial_t\phi(x,0,t)+g\eta(x,t)-\frac{\gamma}{\rho}\Delta_h\eta(x,t)=0.$$

Let $\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[X]/(X^2+1)$, with $i:=[X]$ and $i^2=-1$; this quotient is the complex field. Let $\exp:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be the everywhere-convergent series-defined complex exponential $\exp w:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}w^n/n!$. Let $\pi$ be twice the least positive zero of cosine. For $m=(m_1,m_2)\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ define $\mathbf k:=2\pi(m_1/L_1,m_2/L_2)$ in inverse metres and $k:=|\mathbf k|>0$. For $\omega\in\mathbb C$ in inverse seconds, define on the quotient torus
$$q_m([x],t):=\exp\bigl(i(\mathbf k\cdot\widetilde x-\omega t)\bigr),$$
where $\widetilde x$ is any representative of $[x]$. Changing representatives changes the exponent by $2\pi iN$ for an integer $N$; the exponential addition law and $\exp(i\pi)=-1$ give $\exp(2\pi iN)=1$, so $q_m$ is well-defined. Its lift is smooth and satisfies $\Delta_hq_m=-k^2q_m$.

A nonzero complex mode of angular frequency $\omega$ and index $m$ is a pair $\eta_c:\mathbb T^2_L\times I\to\mathbb C$ and $\phi_c:\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb C$ given by $\eta_c([x],t)=Hq_m([x],t)$ and $\phi_c([x],z,t)=F(z)q_m([x],t)$, satisfying the complex-linear extension of the displayed equations, where $H\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ is in metres and $F\in C^2([-h,0],\mathbb C)$ is in metres squared per second. Here $F$ is continuous on the closed interval, twice continuously differentiable on $(-h,0)$, and its first two derivatives extend continuously to both endpoints. The real and imaginary parts of every such mode solve the real linear model. Such a nonzero mode exists exactly when
$$\omega^2=\left(gk+\frac{\gamma}{\rho}k^3\right)\tanh(kh).$$
For these hypotheses the right-hand side is positive because $k,h,g,\gamma,\rho>0$ and $\tanh(kh)>0$. Thus each $m\ne(0,0)$ admits modes at the two real angular frequencies $\omega=\pm\sqrt{(gk+(\gamma/\rho)k^3)\tanh(kh)}$, with the positive real square root. This is a conditional prediction of the stated first-order model, not a measurement, a finite-amplitude approximation claim, or an assertion that an actual fluid satisfies every assumption.

derivations.claim: At any time $t$ in the model's nonempty interval, the theorem's factor in [F1] is $q_m(x,t)=q_m^h(x)\exp(-i\omega t)$. Its scalar time factor is nonzero by the exponential reciprocal identity, so $\Delta_hq_m=-k^2q_m$ in [F1] gives $\Delta_hq_m^h=-k^2q_m^h$ after cancellation. Linearity then gives $\Delta_h\eta_m=-k^2\eta_m$ for $\eta_m=Hq_m^h$.
By [F1], $\omega^2=k(g+\gamma k^2/\rho)\tanh(kh)>0$ for the nonzero lattice mode defined in the Example; hence each model frequency is real and nonzero.
Since $k>0$, $\gamma>0$, and $\rho>0$, the capillary coefficient $\gamma k^2/\rho$ is positive; adding $g>0$ yields $g+\gamma k^2/\rho>0$.
